thread.title_full: False alarms, new Tusculum City Hall among topics discussed at meeting - NewsBreak

author: Ken Little Sun
title: False alarms, new Tusculum City Hall among topics discussed at meeting - NewsBreak
text:
By Ken Little Sun ,
1 hours ago The Tusculum Board of Mayor and Commissioners meeting Monday night included no new or pending agenda items, but several topics important to residents and commissioners were discussed at length.
False fire alarm activations at Tusculum University, possible solutions to rein in speeding drivers, the status of a proposal for a new city hall building and an update on negotiations with the Federal Emergency Management Agency to receive reimbursement related to Hurricane Helene road damage were all on the table.
Commissioners and Tusculum police Sgt. Josh Kyker also explained the use of an automated license plate reader system. The board could sign a contract next month with a private company to formalize the use of a camera system to track vehicles entering to the city.
FALSE ALARMS
Between Aug. 23 and Sept. 26, a total of 19 false alarm and false calls were received. At least 17 through Monday night in September were “false and malicious” alarms generated in dorms and other college locations, according to the Tusculum Volunteer Fire Department.
Between July 26 and Aug. 22, the Tusculum Volunteer Fire Department received 21 false alarm and false calls, with 15 of them originating on the Tusculum University campus.
Unless notified that the alarms are false by campus security or other university personnel, each call requires a response from the fire department.
Some of the false alarms come in the early morning hours and disrupt the lives of the volunteer firefighters and their families, Vice-Mayor Barbara Britton said. Britton suggested improved communication with the university is needed now that the fall semester is back in session.
“Something has got to be done with that. We (need more) coordination with the college if these calls are coming in from a concentrated area,” she said. “These are volunteers. I think the college should be taking over some of the (call expense) money. Something has got to change.”
Mayor Alan Corley is a member of the Tusculum College Board of Trustees, which next meets on Oct. 15. Corley said he has discussed the matter with university administrators.
“I think we need to take a deeper look at where they are coming from. Is it an alarm system or is it something smoking?” he asked.
Some students use microwave ovens. Kyker inspected some campus dorm rooms and also found hot plates, toaster ovens and other cooking devices. Smoking in the building may also be triggering alarms.
“We are trying to figure out what is going on over there,” he said. “I was under the assumption they only had microwaves.”
Britton asked Corley to relay a message to the university board of trustees.
“Tell them we have got an irate commissioner,” she said.
SPEEDING DRIVERS
Several residents living in a hilly neighborhood along Erwin Highway attended the meeting to express concern about drivers who routinely exceed the 25 mph speed limit. Kyker reported that 52 speeding citations were issued citywide in July, with 26 more being issued in August.
Erwin Highway resident James Ostrow has suggested possible solutions to curb speeding at previous board meetings.
“My mailbox has already been taken out once,” he said.
Speed tables installed in several other locations in Tusculum have helped slow traffic, and Ostrow said they would have the same effect in his neighborhood.
“I think they would absolutely help. This has been an issue we have been talking about for three years,” he said.
A 2025 Erwin Highway traffic count in the area in near Park Avenue down to the 107 Bypass tallied a daily average of 2,167 motorists during a one-week span. The survey found motorists driving at an average speed of 32.3 mph, above the 25 mph speed limit.
Ostrow and several neighbors told commissioners that reckless drivers far exceed the Erwin Highway speed limit every day.
Installing speed tables on several streets in Tusculum have helped slow traffic in problem areas, Kyker said.
CITY HALL PROJECT
After the meeting concluded, Corley provided an update on a long-discussed project to renovate or replace Tusculum City Hall. Tusculum’s population continues to grow, and city departments are running out of space to conduct operations.
The existing structure covers about 1,200 square feet and dates to the early 1960s. The foundation and some walls were shored up about 10 years ago, along with necessary repairs to other sections of the building.
A new or completely remodeled city hall, or one adjacent to the current location at 145 Alexander St. has been considered a top priority for years, but securing funding has delayed the project. An architectural plan was completed several years ago.
A recent workshop on building a new city hall resulted in mission and vision statements, but no solution on a spending plan. The envisioned new city hall would cover about 9,000 square feet at a preliminary estimated cost of about $2.5 million.
“It’s cheaper to do it all together. We looked for grants, we looked for (financing) rates, but it’s still on our wish list,” Corley said.
The new city hall would include expanded police department space, administrative offices, a conference room and a new boardroom for public meetings.
Britton noted the lack of accommodations in the current building for those with disabilities, including suitable parking space outside city hall; and rest room access. She added that traffic and municipal court sessions are held in the cramped public meeting space. Defendants who are assessed fines must walk behind where the judge is seated to access the city recorder’s office.
“I would not sit there. I understand money is an issue, but we also do not have handicapped accessible ramps,” Britton said. “There is no rest room access for handicapped people.”
Commissioners “need to take a serious look at accommodating our citizens with this parking issue,” she said.
Kyker said the Tusculum Police Department has outgrown its current office area in city hall. The police department now numbers three full-time and 10 auxiliary officers.
“We would absolutely love it. We would be super excited,” he said about a new city hall. Until that time, “We will make do,” Kyker added.
Corley said the city would be able to fund about half of the project expense, but a means of securing remaining funding as construction costs increase remains a challenge.
“We have explored some funding sources,” he said.
Improved access for those with disabilities should be an immediate priority, Britton said.
Paved parking spaces where shrubs are now planted could address the situation, Corley said.
“We will do something,” he said.
ROAD REPAIR RELIEF
Tusculum officials are still waiting for an update from the Federal Emergency Management Agency, which initially indicated it would provide funds to reimburse the city for repairing road damage from trucks hauling storm debris caused two years ago by Hurricane Helene.
City Recorder Randy Harley said the initial request took six months to process and was rejected along with a subsequent appeal to FEMA. The federal agency told city leaders the request for reimbursement was not filed “in a timely manner,” but Harley said the extent of road damage did not become apparent until the spring of 2025, after tons of debris were removed from areas devastated by flooding.
Streets that sustained extensive damage from trucks hauling heavy loads include Shiloh, Cumberland and Greenwood roads.
“The governor has the money. I made the decision to go forward with arbitration,” Harley said.
The city suspended road paving work as the arbitration process with FEMA proceeds.
TVFD OPEN HOUSE
In other business, Corley reminded the public about upcoming Tusculum Volunteer Fire Department events and activities.
The fire department will host an open house from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Saturday, Oct. 10, at the fire station, 150 Alexander St, in recognition of National Fire Prevention Week. Food will be available and there will be an extrication demonstration at 1 p.m., along with equipment displays and information for the public.
Tusculum firefighters will hold their annual “roadblock” fundraiser at several locations on Saturday, Oct. 17.
The fire department will host its annual Halloween trick or treat event for the public from 5:30 to 9 p.m. on Saturday, Oct. 31, at the fire station. Candy for trick-or-treaters will be distributed, along with an opportunity to meet firefighters and have a photo taken on a fire truck. The Tusculum Police Department and city Public Works Department will also participate in handing out treats.
summary: False fire alarm activations at Tusculum University, possible solutions to rein in speeding drivers, the status of a proposal for a new city hall building and an update on negotiations with the Federal Emergency Management Agency to receive reimbursement related to Hurricane Helene road damage were all on the table. Several residents living in a hilly neighborhood along Erwin Highway attended the meeting to express concern about drivers who routinely exceed the 25 mph speed limit.
